newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian central bank limits non-cash dollar use.
newsitem.headline: Russian central bank limits non-cash dollar use.

text.p: Russia's central bank, in its latest move to "de-dollarise" the economy, is to stop granting companies permission to accept non-cash payments in foreign currency as of June 1, a spokeswoman said on Friday.

While payment for goods and services in foreign cash was outlawed at the beginning of 1994, the Central Bank has continued to allow non-cash transactions -- for example credit card purchases -- in foreign currencies.
A statement from the bank's Moscow branch said current permits would remain in effect until further notice.
"As of June 1, 1997 the issuing of permits to legal entities to sell goods (work, services) to citizens for foreign currency on the territory of the Russian Federation will cease," it said.
The Central Bank statement said it had issued 2,365 permit in the Moscow area alone.

The U.S. dollar retains a prominent place in the Russian economy six years after the start of economic reforms which sent the rouble into a nose dive and Russians scrambling to exchange roubles for hard currency.
Prices for goods and services are often quoted in dollars, but with its latest move the Central Bank has added yet another plank to the supporting structure of the rouble.
"The Central Bank of Russia works to provide for the strength of the national currency," said Svetlana Orlova, a press spokesman for the bank's Moscow branch.
"Its steps have been and in the future will be aimed at securing the stability of the rouble exchange rate."
Inflation is expected to drop to 12 percent this year from about 22 percent in 1996 and 131 percent in 1995.
Pushing back inflation is central to the government's plan to make the rouble, which does not trade outside Russia and some former Soviet republics, fully convertible by 2000.
But it may be some time before Russians, who hold about $20 billion in dollars, are fully at home with their own currency.
